theorems.title: How to inscribe a triangle of given angles
theorems.statement: How to inscribe in a circle a triangle that is equiangular with a given triangle.

steps.text: Let the given triangle have angles 1, 2, 3, and let K be the given circle. Draw a tangent TPN touching K at P.
At P make ∠TPA = ∠2 and ∠NPB = ∠1, with A and B on the circumference.
Join AB. The remaining angle at P of triangle APB equals ∠3, since the three angles at P on the straight line plus ∠APB are two right angles, as are ∠1+∠2+∠3.
By the alternate-segment theorem, ∠TPA = ∠ABP and ∠NPB = ∠BAP.
Therefore triangle APB is equiangular with the given triangle.

theorems.title: How to circumscribe a triangle of given angles
theorems.statement: How to circumscribe about a circle a triangle that is equiangular with a given triangle.

steps.text: At the center M of the given circle, make three adjacent angles equal to the supplements of the given triangle’s angles (so they fill the space around M).
The rays cut the circle at F, R, G. At those points draw tangents; they form a triangle.
Each tangent is perpendicular to the radius (Ch.3 Thm. 15). The angles of the tangent triangle are therefore equal to the given angles.

theorems.title: How to inscribe a circle in a triangle
theorems.statement: How to inscribe a circle in any triangle.

steps.text: Bisect two angles of the given triangle ABC; let the bisectors meet at I.
Drop a perpendicular from I to a side, meeting it at D. With centre I and radius ID describe a circle.
A point on an angle bisector is equidistant from the sides, so the perpendiculars to all three sides are equal, and the circle touches all three.

remarks: The three angle bisectors of a triangle meet in one point — the incenter.

theorems.title: How to circumscribe a circle about a triangle
theorems.statement: How to circumscribe a circle about any triangle.

steps.text: Draw the perpendicular bisectors of two sides of triangle ABC; let them meet at O.
With centre O and radius OA describe a circle.
O is equidistant from A, B, and C, so the circle passes through all three vertices.

remarks: The three perpendicular bisectors meet in one point — the circumcenter.

theorems.title: How to inscribe a square in a circle
theorems.statement: How to inscribe a square in any circle.

steps.text: Draw a diameter AC of the given circle.
Through the center draw BD perpendicular to AC, meeting the circle at B and D.
Join ABCD. The four right angles at the center are equal, the four radii are equal, so ABCD is equilateral and right-angled — a square.

theorems.title: The golden isosceles triangle
theorems.statement: How to make an isosceles triangle whose base angles are each double the remaining angle.

steps.text: Take a line AB and cut it at C so that AB · BC = AC² (Ch.2 Thm. 12 / Euclid II.11).
On AB construct equilateral-style: with centre A and radius AB, and centre B and radius AB, take D on the first circle so that BD = AC.
Join AD, DC. Triangle ABD is isosceles with AB = AD, and the cut makes each base angle double the vertex.

remarks: This triangle is the building-block of the regular pentagon: 36° at the vertex, 72° at the base.

theorems.title: How to inscribe a regular pentagon
theorems.statement: How to inscribe a regular pentagon inside any circle.

steps.text: In the given circle, construct the isosceles triangle of Theorem 6, with vertex at the center or inscribed so its vertex angle stands on one fifth of the circumference.
The base of that triangle subtends two-fifths of the circumference; stepping that chord around the circle five times closes a regular pentagon.
All sides are equal chords on equal arcs, and all angles stand on equal remaining arcs, so the pentagon is equilateral and equiangular.

theorems.title: How to inscribe a regular hexagon
theorems.statement: How to inscribe a regular hexagon inside any circle.

steps.text: Take a radius of the given circle and, starting at any point A on the circumference, mark off six equal chords each equal to the radius.
Each such chord subtends 60° at the center (equilateral triangle with two radii). Six of them fill 360° and close the figure.
The hexagon is equilateral and equiangular.

theorems.title: How to inscribe a regular decagon
theorems.statement: How to inscribe a regular decagon in any circle.

steps.text: The golden triangle of Theorem 6 has vertex 36°. Placed at the center of the circle, that angle cuts off one tenth of the circumference.
The chord of that arc, stepped ten times around the circle, is a regular decagon.

extra.text: A right triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 can be inscribed in a circle whose diameter is the hypotenuse 5. The same circle makes a neat playground for integer chords and for showing that not every inscribed right triangle is isosceles.
extra.kid: A hook — the friendliest Pythagorean triple sitting in a circle.

extra.text: If a hexagon is circumscribed about a circle (every side tangent), then the three lines joining opposite vertices meet in a single point. Dual to Pascal’s theorem on a hexagon inscribed in a conic.
extra.kid: A hook for projective geometry later on.

extra.text: In a regular n-gon inscribed in a unit circle, the product of the lengths of the chords from one vertex to all the others is n. A surprising arithmetic hiding in the polygon.
